title: Bhai Gurdas, the man
hookLine: the scribe who, tradition says, was once tested and forgiven by Guru Hargobind

lines: FIND MY THIEF AND TIE HIS HANDS.
cards: A letter arrives at a king's court in Banaras, far from Punjab. It's from Guru Hargobind, and it says something strange: a thief of mine is hiding in your city. Find him, tie his hands, and send him back to me.
The king's men go looking. Before they find anyone, a quiet, learned man steps forward and says: that's me. I'm the one he means.
The thief is the Guru's own scribe.

teach.b: Bhai Gurdas is a name this path has met as a writer. Tradition says he wrote out the Granth as Guru Arjan dictated it, and Sikhs speak of his own Vars as a key to the Guru's word.
So it's a surprise that the story Sikhs tell about him as a man is a story of failure. There's more than one version.

teach.h: SENT TO KABUL, THE MONEY GONE.
teach.b: In a well-known one, Guru Hargobind sent him to Kabul with money to buy horses. He made the bargain and went into his tent to fetch the payment, and the money wasn't there. Some tellings say it had turned to stones.
With the dealers waiting outside, he panicked. He was the Guru's trusted man, and he couldn't pay.
So he slipped out the back of the tent and ran, all the way to Banaras, where nobody knew him. Some tellings add a reason for the test: he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver.
Then came the letter about the thief. He knew at once who was meant.
He gave himself up and was led back with his hands tied. Before Guru Hargobind, tradition says, he answered in verse, admitting he had failed and asking for mercy the way a child asks a parent.
The Guru forgave him, and he stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life. Sikhs didn't hide this story to protect a great name. They kept it.
The man tradition credits with writing out the Granth was tested, ran, came back, and was forgiven.

how: Sikhs honor Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Granth and the author of the Vars, which are sung in gurdwaras, and they tell the story of his test and forgiveness as part of who he was.

s: Sikh tradition left out the story of Bhai Gurdas's failure to protect his name
Sikhs kept the story and still tell it.
the Guru's letter asked for a thief to be tied and sent back
and Bhai Gurdas stepped forward and said the thief was him.
after he came back, Bhai Gurdas was sent away from the Guru's house

games.q: you're Bhai Gurdas in Banaras. the king's men are looking for the Guru's thief, and you know it's you. what do you do?
o: leave the city before they find you.
step forward and say it's you.
write to the Guru explaining why it wasn't your fault.
games.why: tradition says he gave himself up, went back with his hands tied, admitted his failure in verse, and was forgiven.

practice: Bring to mind one person who let you down in a small way recently: a late reply, a dropped promise, a moment they ran instead of facing something.
Don't replay it; just see them, the way Guru Hargobind saw a frightened man with tied hands, and notice whether you've been keeping them in the thief's role.
On each breath out, loosen the knot a little, and if you pray, say Waheguru with it.

wordCard.voice: Bhai Gurdas. The scribe and poet who, tradition says, failed a test, ran, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven by Guru Hargobind.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bhai Gurdas; Bhai, brother, is a title of respect for a learned or devoted Sikh.

carryVoice: Your line: even he was tested. Running wasn't the end of his story. Rest well.
